Real-valued pressure perturbation p(x,t) and particle velocity u(x,t), forming q(x,t) = (p(x,t),u(x,t)) in ℝ² [printed p. 2, (1.5)–(1.6)].
Constant material parameters K, the bulk modulus of compressibility, and ρ, the density [printed p. 2, paragraph following (1.5)].
For the surrounding integral interpretation, any two spatial endpoints x₁ and x₂ [printed p. 4, (1.10), 'for any two points'].
hypotheses: p and u satisfy the constant-coefficient linear acoustic equations p_t + K u_x = 0 and u_t + (1/ρ)p_x = 0 [printed p. 2, (1.5); printed p. 4, selected acoustics sentence].
K and ρ are independent of space and time, as material constants in the selected constant-coefficient system [printed p. 2, paragraph following (1.5); printed p. 4, 'constant-coefficient'].

The differential expressions require the relevant partial derivatives; sufficient smoothness is explicitly required in the surrounding discussion when deriving differential form from integral form, without a specified function class [printed p. 1, derivative convention following (1.1); printed p. 4, Section 1.1.2].
conclusions: The constant-coefficient linear acoustic equations are conservation laws for pressure and velocity [printed p. 4, selected sentence in Section 1.1.1].

Specializing the explicitly stated linear flux f(q) = Aq to the acoustic state and matrix gives f(p,u) = (Ku,p/ρ); consequently their differential conservation form is p_t + ∂_x(Ku) = 0 and u_t + ∂_x(p/ρ) = 0. This explicit component flux is an algebraic inference from the source formulas [printed p. 2, (1.6); printed pp. 3–4, (1.8) and 'linear flux function f(q) = Aq'].

The mathematical conservation-law description does not assert exact physical conservation of pressure and velocity: the source gives only an approximate physical interpretation for very small amplitude disturbances in uniform media [printed p. 4, sentence beginning 'Physically, however'].
definitions_and_conventions: The state order is q = (p,u), with matrix A having rows (0,K) and (1/ρ,0) [printed p. 2, (1.6)].
p denotes pressure, more properly its perturbation from a constant background pressure; u denotes particle velocity [printed p. 2, paragraph following (1.5)].
Subscripts t and x denote partial derivatives with respect to time and space [printed p. 1, paragraph following (1.1)].
Differential conservation-law form means q_t + ∂_x(f(q)) = 0, where f is the flux function [printed p. 3, (1.8)].
The surrounding integral convention uses left endpoint flux minus right endpoint flux: d/dt ∫ from x₁ to x₂ q dx = f(q(x₁,t)) − f(q(x₂,t)) [printed p. 4, (1.10)].
implicit_context: The setting is a first-order system in one space dimension; the acoustic system models waves propagating in both directions along a one-dimensional medium [printed p. 1, introduction to (1.1); printed p. 2, introduction to (1.5)].

The selected assertion applies the preceding general observation that a constant-coefficient linear system is a conservation law with flux Aq [printed pp. 3–4, sentence spanning the page break after (1.9)].

The very small amplitude and uniform-medium qualification concerns physical conservation, as signaled by 'Physically, however'; it is not separately stated as a hypothesis needed for the algebraic flux rewriting [printed p. 4, selected paragraph].

details: The two conserved state components in the formal PDE description are pressure and velocity themselves, in that order [printed p. 4, selected sentence; printed p. 2, (1.6)].
Their associated component fluxes are Ku and p/ρ, inferred from the acoustic matrix and the prescribed flux Aq [printed p. 2, (1.6); printed p. 4, opening sentence].

Constancy of the coefficients permits moving K and 1/ρ inside spatial derivatives; no variable-coefficient version is asserted here [printed p. 4, 'constant-coefficient linear acoustics equations'; printed p. 2, (1.5)].

The surrounding conservation-law interpretation describes interval totals changing through endpoint fluxes, not unconditional constancy of those totals [printed p. 4, (1.10) and its explanatory paragraph].

Specialization of (1.10) gives endpoint terms K u(x₁,t) − K u(x₂,t) for pressure and p(x₁,t)/ρ − p(x₂,t)/ρ for velocity; this is an inferred specialization, not a separately displayed acoustic equation [printed p. 4, (1.10); printed p. 2, (1.6)].
Approximate physical conservation is restricted to very small amplitude disturbances in uniform media [printed p. 4, 'Physically, however'].

The following discussion distinguishes this acoustic model from the Euler equations, which model conservation of mass, momentum, and energy [printed p. 4, acoustics paragraph, 'These equations model the conservation of mass, momentum, and energy'].

Preserve the coefficients: pressure flux Ku and velocity flux p/ρ follow from the specified matrix and flux Aq [printed p. 2, (1.6); printed p. 4, opening sentence].
Preserve the constant-coefficient scope [printed p. 4, 'constant-coefficient linear acoustics equations (1.5)'].
Do not turn the approximate physical interpretation into exact physical conservation [printed p. 4, 'not conserved quantities except approximately'].

contract_plain_english: For the one-dimensional acoustic system p_t + K u_x = 0 and u_t + (1/ρ)p_x = 0 with constant material parameters, the source asserts that pressure and particle velocity admit a conservation-law description. Combining the state and matrix in (1.6) with the stated linear flux f(q) = Aq yields the component fluxes Ku and p/ρ, hence p_t + ∂_x(Ku) = 0 and u_t + ∂_x(p/ρ) = 0 [printed p. 2, (1.5)–(1.6); printed pp. 3–4, (1.8) and the linear-flux sentence]. The surrounding integral description expresses changes in interval totals through endpoint flux differences [printed p. 4, (1.10)]. The selected paragraph separately states that pressure and velocity are physically conserved only approximately for very small amplitude disturbances in uniform media [printed p. 4, Section 1.1.1, acoustics paragraph].
